item.title: Go Daily Question 20250610
item.description:
Regarding goroutines, which of the following statements are correct? ()

  • B. Threads are more lightweight than goroutines;
  • C. Goroutines do not have deadlock issues;

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250609
item.description:
What is the output value of counter in the following code?

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var m = map[string]int{
		"A": 21,
		"B": 22,
		"C": 23,
	}
	counter := 0
	for k, v := range m {
		if counter == 0 {
			delete(m, "A")
		}
		counter++
		fmt.Println(k, v)
	}
	fmt.Println("counter is ", counter)
}
  • A. 2
  • B. 3
  • C. 2 or 3
🔑 Answer Analysis:

C Go Online Run The iteration order of for range map is unordered. If A is encountered in the first iteration, the output is 3; otherwise, it is 2.

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250608
item.description:
What is the output of the following code? Why?

package main

import "fmt"

type Foo struct {
    bar string
}

func main() {
    s1 := []Foo{
        {"A"},
        {"B"},
        {"C"},
    }
    s2 := make([]*Foo, len(s1))
    for i, value := range s1 {
        s2[i] = &value
    }
    fmt.Println(s1[0], s1[1], s1[2])
    fmt.Println(s2[0], s2[1], s2[2])
}

// Output:
// {A} {B} {C}
// &{A} &{B} &{C}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Go Online Run

The answer to this question depends on the Go version. For Go versions < 1.22, the output is:

// Output:
// {A} {B} {C}
// &{C} &{C} &{C}

For versions 1.22 and later, the output is:

// Output:
// {A} {B} {C}
// &{A} &{B} &{C}

Before Go 1.22, in for i, value := range s1, the address of value would be reused. The addresses recorded by s2[i] = &value would all be the same address. The content of value changes with each loop iteration until it iterates to the last value, which is {C}.

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250607
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var a = []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
    var r [5]int

    for i, v := range a {
        if i == 0 {
            a[1] = 12
            a[2] = 13
        }
        r[i] = v
    }
    fmt.Println("r = ", r)
    fmt.Println("a = ", a)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis: 
r =  [1 12 13 4 5]
a =  [1 12 13 4 5]

Go Online Run

Although it iterates over a copy of a, as long as no reallocation occurs, both the copy and a point to the same underlying array, thus the content of a can be modified.

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250606
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

func hello(i int) {
       fmt.Println(i)
}
func main() {
       i := 5
       defer hello(i)
       i = i + 10
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

5 Run online Go parameters are passed by value only. When defer hello(i) is executed, the value of i is already determined.

Below is the structure of _defer:

type _defer struct {
       heap      bool
       rangefunc bool    // true for rangefunc list
       sp        uintptr // sp at time of defer
       pc        uintptr // pc at time of defer
       fn        func()  // can be nil for open-coded defers
       link      *_defer // next defer on G; can point to either heap or stack!

       // If rangefunc is true, *head is the head of the atomic linked list
       // during a range-over-func execution.
       head *atomic.Pointer[_defer]
}

The registration of defer essentially calls the built-in function runtime.deferproc.

func deferproc(siz int32, fn *funcval)
  • siz int32:
    • Represents the total size of the defer function’s arguments (in bytes).
    • Used to allocate enough space on the stack to save arguments.
  • fn *funcval:
    • Represents the function value of the defer function (including the function pointer and captured arguments).
    • funcval is a runtime internal struct used to represent function metadata.

Therefore, we can conclude that the captured parameters are already determined at the time of registration.

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250605
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

package main

import (
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	var a = [5]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
	var r [5]int

	for i, v := range a {
		if i == 0 {
			a[1] = 12
			a[2] = 13
		}
		r[i] = v
	}
	fmt.Println("r = ", r)
	fmt.Println("a = ", a)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis: 
r =  [1 2 3 4 5]
a =  [1 12 13 4 5]

Go Online Run

Array range behavior: When using range to iterate over an array, Go first creates a copy of the original array, and the iteration is performed on this copy. Therefore, modifications to the original array within the loop will not affect the values during iteration.

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250604
item.description:
What does the following code output?

package main

import "fmt"

func f(n int) (r int) {
    defer func() {
        r += n
        recover()
    }()

    var f func()

    defer f()
    
    f = func() {
        r += 2
    }
    return n + 1
}

func main() {
    fmt.Println(f(3))
}
🔑 Solution Analysis:

7

// First execute this code, then r is assigned the value 4
return n+1

// Then it executes, but triggers a panic
defer f()

// Finally it executes, r increases by 3, r=7, then recover(), and the function returns 7
defer func() {
        r += n
        recover()
    }()

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250603
item.description:

    time.Sleep(time.Second * 3)

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250602
item.description:
Will the following code terminate normally?

func main() {
    v := []int{1, 2, 3}
    for i := range v {
        v = append(v, i)
    }
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

It will not result in an infinite loop and will terminate normally.

The number of iterations is determined before the loop starts. Changing the length of the slice within the loop does not affect the number of iterations.

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250601
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

var p *int

func foo() (*int, error) {
    var i int = 5
    return &i, nil
}

func bar() {
    //use p
    fmt.Println(*p)
}

func main() {
    p, err := foo()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Println(err)
        return
    }
    bar()
    fmt.Println(*p)
}

A. 5 5 B. runtime error

🔑 Answer Analysis:

B The global *p is nil. In p, err := foo(), p here is a new local variable and is unrelated to the global p.
